title: Chapter 18 — His Mark
paragraphs: As we walked down the wharf toward the ship, Queequeg carrying his harpoon, Captain Peleg loudly called out to us from his wigwam in his gruff voice. He said he hadn't realized my friend was a cannibal, and he didn't allow any cannibals on board unless they could produce their papers first.
"What do you mean by that, Captain Peleg?" said I, jumping up onto the ship's rail and leaving my companion standing on the wharf.
"I mean," he replied, "he has to show his papers."

"Yes," said Captain Bildad in his hollow voice, poking his head out from behind Peleg's in the wigwam. "He must prove he's been converted. Son of darkness," he added, turning to Queequeg, "are you currently in communion with any Christian church?"
"Why," said I, "he's a member of the First Congregational Church." Let it be said here that many tattooed savages who sail in Nantucket ships end up at last being converted into the churches.

"First Congregational Church!" cried Bildad. "What! The one that meets in Deacon Deuteronomy Coleman's meeting house?" And saying this, he took out his spectacles, wiped them with his big yellow handkerchief, put them on very carefully, came out of the wigwam, and, leaning stiffly over the rail, took a good long look at Queequeg.
"How long has he been a member?" he then said, turning to me. "Not very long, I'd guess, young man."
"No," said Peleg, "and he hasn't been properly baptized either, or it would have washed some of that devil's blue off his face."
"Is that so?" cried Bildad. "Is this Philistine really a member of Deacon Deuteronomy's congregation? I never saw him there, and I pass it every Lord's day."
"I don't know anything about Deacon Deuteronomy or his meeting," said I. "All I know is that Queequeg here is a born member of the First Congregational Church. He's a deacon himself, Queequeg is."
"Young man," said Bildad sternly, "you are skylarking with me — explain yourself, you young Hittite. What church do you mean? Answer me."

Finding myself pushed this hard, I replied, "I mean, sir, the same ancient Catholic — that is, universal — Church to which you and I, and Captain Peleg there, and Queequeg here, and all of us, every mother's son and soul of us, belong: the great and everlasting First Congregation of this whole worshipping world. We all belong to that; only some of us cherish some odd crotchets that in no way touch the grand belief. In that, at least, we all join hands."

"Splice — you mean splice hands," cried Peleg, coming closer. "Young man, you'd better sign on as a missionary instead of a common sailor. I never heard a better sermon. Deacon Deuteronomy — why, Father Mapple himself couldn't beat it, and he's considered something. Come aboard, come aboard — never mind about the papers. I say, tell Quohog there — what do you call him? Tell Quohog to step along. By the great anchor, what a harpoon he's got there! Looks like good stuff, that, and he handles it just right. I say, Quohog, or whatever your name is, have you ever stood in the bow of a whale-boat? Have you ever struck a whale?"

Without saying a word, Queequeg, in his wild way, jumped up onto the ship's rail, from there into the bow of one of the whale-boats hanging alongside, and then, bracing his left knee and balancing his harpoon, cried out something like this:

"Cap'ain, you see him small drop tar on water there? You see him? Well, s'pose him one whale eye — well, then!" And taking sharp aim at it, he darted the iron right over old Bildad's broad brim, clean across the ship's decks, and struck the glistening tar spot out of sight.
"Now," said Queequeg, calmly hauling in the line, "suppose that whale eye. Well, then — that whale dead."

"Quick, Bildad," said Peleg, his partner, who had retreated toward the cabin entrance, shaken by how close the flying harpoon had come. "Quick, I say, Bildad — get the ship's papers. We need Hedgehog there — I mean Quohog — in one of our boats. Listen, Quohog, we'll give you the ninetieth lay, and that's more than any harpooner out of Nantucket has ever been given."
So down we went into the cabin, and to my great joy, Queequeg was soon enrolled in the same ship's company as me.

When all the formalities were done and Peleg had everything ready for signing, he turned to me and said, "I guess Quohog there doesn't know how to write, does he? I say, Quohog — blast you! Do you sign your name or make your mark?"

But Queequeg, who had taken part in similar ceremonies two or three times before, looked not at all embarrassed. Taking the offered pen, he copied onto the paper, in the proper place, an exact replica of a strange round figure tattooed on his arm. So, thanks to Captain Peleg's stubborn error with his name, it looked something like this:
Quohog. his X mark.

Meanwhile, Captain Bildad sat earnestly and steadfastly eyeing Queequeg. At last he rose solemnly, fumbled in the huge pockets of his broad-skirted drab coat, and pulled out a bundle of tracts. Selecting one titled "The Latter Day Coming; or No Time to Lose," he placed it in Queequeg's hands. Then, grasping those hands and the tract with both of his own, he looked earnestly into his eyes and said, "Son of darkness, I must do my duty by you. I am part owner of this ship, and I feel concerned for the souls of all its crew. If you still cling to your Pagan ways, which I sadly fear, I beg you, do not remain forever a bondsman of Belial. Spurn the idol Bell, and the hideous dragon; turn from the wrath to come; mind your eye, I say; oh! goodness gracious! steer clear of the fiery pit!"
Something of the salt sea still lingered in old Bildad's speech, oddly mixed with scriptural and domestic phrases.

"Hold on there, hold on there, Bildad — stop spoiling our harpooner," cried Peleg. "Pious harpooners never make good voyagers — it takes the shark out of them; no harpooner is worth a straw who isn't pretty sharkish. There was young Nat Swaine, once the bravest boat-header out of all Nantucket and the Vineyard; he joined the meeting, and never came to any good. He got so frightened about his plaguy soul that he shrank and sheered away from whales, for fear of what might come after, in case he got stove and went to Davy Jones."

"Peleg! Peleg!" said Bildad, lifting his eyes and hands. "You yourself, as well as I, have seen many a perilous time. You know, Peleg, what it is to have the fear of death. How, then, can you prattle in this ungodly way? You belie your own heart, Peleg. Tell me — when this same Pequod here had her three masts overboard in that typhoon off Japan, that same voyage when you went as mate with Captain Ahab, didn't you think of Death and the Judgment then?"

"Hear him! Hear him now!" cried Peleg, marching across the cabin and thrusting his hands deep into his pockets. "Hear him, all of you. Think of that! When every moment we thought the ship would go down! Death and the Judgment then? What? With all three masts making such an endless thundering against the hull, and every wave breaking over us fore and aft? Think of Death and the Judgment then? No! No time to think about death. Life was what Captain Ahab and I were thinking about — and how to save every hand on board. How to rig jury-masts (makeshift masts). How to reach the nearest port. That was what I was thinking about."

Bildad said no more. He buttoned up his coat and walked out on deck, where we followed him. There he stood, very quietly watching some sailmakers who were mending a topsail amidships. Now and then he stooped to pick up a patch or save a length of tarred twine that might otherwise have been wasted.
